#10262. 10 Best AI App Builders I've Used in 2026 (and What Each One Gets Wrong)

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI App Builders are exploding in popularity, and for good reason. It’s never been easier to build real, functional apps and internal tools using app builders. To test them all, I built the same app on 10 of the most popular AI app builders and tested each across usability, cost, correctness, and ease of use. Most of them can turn a paragraph of description into something that looks like software within a single session. The differences show up around the tenth prompt, when you learn what each edit costs and who has to fix the code once something breaks. I took every price from the vendor's own pricing page on October 29, 2026.

TLDR: Of the best AI app builders I've used, Softr is the one I'd hand to a team that needs auth, data, user groups or integrations. The other nine I tested include code generators such as Lovable and Bolt and visual platforms such as Bubble and Glide, and each one carries a cost or upkeep trade-off worth seeing before you commit.

I looked at the same seven things in every tool, from the first prompt onward:

Softr gets used a lot by operations and business teams as their AI app builder for secure client portals, internal tools and other business apps, none of which require code. Write a short brief in your own words, and the AI Co-Builder turns it into a database plus the core app that sits on it: tables, pages and layouts, the data connections behind them, plus user groups and permissions, so real users can sign in from day one. Workflows come as the next step, either by prompting the Co-Builder again or by adding them in the visual editor.

The Free plan is $0 for unlimited apps, with room for 5 app users, 3 builders, 5,000 records and 5 AI credits each month. Basic runs $19 per month, Pro $99 and Business $329, all on annual billing. Enterprise pricing is custom and includes SSO and SCIM for organizations managing access at scale. The full plan table sits on Softr's pricing page.

Lovable builds full-stack web apps through conversation, writing React code while it takes care of hosting, SSL and the backend. It's designed to move a founder or product team from a prompt to a shareable prototype, and the preview updates as the agent works.

Base44 calls itself a no-code AI platform: you explain the app, and it generates the structure, design and logic while running the backend itself. Authentication, a database and analytics come on every plan, Free included.

Base44 is free for 25 message credits a month. Starter costs $16 per month and Builder $40 per month, both on annual billing, with Pro at $80 and Elite at $160.

Bolt is a coding agent that writes full-stack projects in the browser and runs them on Bolt Cloud, which supplies hosting, databases and integrations. It suits people who want to watch the code take shape and edit it themselves.

Bolt Free is $0 with 1M tokens a month and Bolt branding. Pro costs $25 per month with 10M tokens, and Teams runs $30 a month for each member on monthly billing.

Replit pairs its Agent with a cloud workspace, so a description turns into a running app whose sign-in, database, hosting and monitoring come wired up. The homepage pitches it to people who don't code, though the result underneath is a code project.

Core costs $20 per month ($18 with annual billing) and Pro costs $100 per month ($90 with annual billing). Enterprise is custom and adds SSO, SCIM and audit logs.

Glide starts internal business apps from whatever you hand it, whether a spreadsheet, a written prompt or a PDF, and its newer platform, GlideOS, reads a sheet's structure and relationships to draft screens and workflows. Its apps grew up on phones, and that heritage still shapes the product.

Glide Free is $0 with limited credits. Basic costs $25 per month, Plus $50 per month and Pro $125 per month; annual billing isn't offered yet, according to Glide.

Bubble Free gives you 50K workload units and 500 AI credits each month. Web plans run $32 per month for Starter, $119 for Growth and $349 for Team, all on annual billing.

Retool is an internal tools engine aimed at engineering teams. You describe or assemble an app that connects straight to production databases, APIs and LLMs, with auth and access controls in place at deployment.

v0 generates full-stack Next.js web apps from a prompt and deploys them to Vercel, with Design Mode for visual tweaks and GitHub sync for the code. It's designed around a developer's workflow.

v0's Free plan gives new users $5 of one-time credits and caps messages at 7 per day. Plus runs $30 a month per user, and Business $100 a month per user.

Figma Make turns prompts and Figma design context into code-backed prototypes and web apps you can publish at a URL. It can also scaffold a Payload backend with a database, APIs, auth and an admin panel, or connect to Supabase for sign-in and stored data.

Figma's Starter plan is free with up to 500 AI credits a month. Figma lists a Professional Full seat at $16 per month with 3,000 AI credits, and Organization Full seats cost $55 per month on annual billing.

Collins Dictionary named "vibe coding" its Word of the Year for 2025, and the phrase now covers any workflow where you describe software in plain language and an AI produces it. AI app builders package that workflow with hosting, data and sign-in, so a non-developer can get from idea to something clickable without installing anything.

The questions buyers ask have turned plainer since then: what each edit costs, who keeps the app running, and whether a client can sign in and see their own records alone. A generated front end makes a good demo, and a team using it every day needs permissions and a predictable bill for the next hundred edits.

Softr is now my default when recommending AI app builders. It handles teams, auth, and real company data better than any other product. The AI Co-Builder drafts tables, pages and user groups, workflows follow as the next step, and the app keeps running on maintained platform components with no codebase to patch. App-user pricing and an editor that works without AI credits keep later changes from turning into a running meter.

Three situations call for a different tool. Glide makes a better mobile-first choice when the app spends its days on phones in the field. Bubble gives more front-end design freedom when a project calls for bespoke layouts, interactive animation or heavy brand styling. If your engineers want version control and audit logs and can handle a technical setup, Retool covers that need.

Agents are moving inside the apps these tools produce. Gartner expects task-specific AI agents inside 40% of enterprise applications by the close of 2026, against under 5% in 2025, so a 2027 app builder will need to host agents that respect the same permissions as human users.

Building is also leaving the builder's own window. The Model Context Protocol now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation and reports more than 97 million SDK downloads a month, with client support in ChatGPT and Claude, among others. Softr's changelog dates its official Claude and ChatGPT connector to October 6, 2026, and I expect more teams to start an app from the chat assistant they already use.

The caution comes from Gartner too: it predicts organizations will scrap upward of 40% of agentic AI projects before 2028, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Going into 2027, I'd judge any builder on whether it keeps agent costs and access rules visible to the team running the app.

Neville Naidoo is a technology journalist covering AI, startups, and the digital economy, with a focus on how emerging technologies are constantly evolving and shaping our everyday life.

#10256. Top 6 AI Detector Tools in 2026: Features, Accuracy Claims and When to Trust Them

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI writing tools are now part of everyday work for students, marketers, developers and editors, and a parallel category of tools has appeared to answer one question: was this text written by a person or a model? Teachers, publishers, hiring teams and content managers use these detectors to screen submissions, but the technology is probabilistic, its accuracy claims vary, and the cost of a wrong call can be high.

This guide compares six AI detector tools, CudekAI, GPTZero, Copyleaks, Originality.ai, Turnitin and Sapling, on what their own pages state. It then explains how detectors work, summarizes the research on their limits, and ends with a short script you can use to test any detector on your own samples. The tools are listed in no ranking order. Feature details, limits and prices change often, so confirm current information on each vendor’s site before you commit.

• A detector gives a probability, not proof. Every vendor in this list warns that results can be wrong, and several advise against using a score alone.

• Limits differ widely. Character limits, supported languages, models detected and free allowances vary between tools and even between pages of the same tool.

• Bias and short text are known weak spots. Research has found detectors misclassify some non-native English writing, and most vendors say accuracy improves with longer text.

• Vendor accuracy claims are not comparable. Figures come from different datasets, thresholds and models, so test on your own material.

• Use detection as one signal. Combine it with drafts, version history, interviews or other evidence before acting on a result.

CudekAI’s AI detector returns an AI percentage and a human percentage for pasted text, with paragraph, sentence and word-level analysis for mixed documents. According to its page, it also accepts PDF and Word files with per-page scores and downloadable reports, and offers separate code and image detectors. The page lists models it says it detects, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, DeepSeek and Grok, and says it supports more than 100 languages.

Strengths: sentence-level highlighting, file uploads with reports, and extra detectors for code and images in the same product.

Limitations and gaps: the page shows different character limits in different places, including 1,000, 5,000 and 15,000, so check the limit that applies to your plan. It says to start free but does not state a free allowance, and it lists detection as costing one credit. A headline accuracy figure of 99 percent appears in its page metadata, while the body refers to independent benchmarking without naming sources, and its FAQ says accuracy may vary for mixed or paraphrased text and that false positives can occur. API access is listed under an enterprise plan.

Fits: writers and teams who want a quick check with sentence-level detail and file reports, and who will verify results rather than rely on a single percentage.

GPTZero gives an overall score and highlights flagged sentences, and adds a Writing Replay feature that records the writing process, including typing patterns and paste events. It also lists a plagiarism checker and integrations with Google Docs, Google Classroom, Canvas, Zapier and a Chrome extension, plus an API.

Strengths: process-based evidence through Writing Replay, strong education integrations and published benchmark figures. On the RAID benchmark, the page reports 95.7 percent of AI text detected and 1 percent of human text wrongly flagged.

Limitations and gaps: it claims full support for five languages (English, German, Portuguese, French and Spanish) and says other languages lack stated accuracy levels. The company’s own page says no detector is 100 percent accurate, that results should not be the final verdict, and that accuracy is higher on longer English text. The free scan box has a 10,000-character limit, and plan prices are not listed on the page.

Fits: educators and editors who want writing-process evidence as well as a score.

Copyleaks describes an AI detector covering more than 30 languages and models including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek and Llama. Its AI Logic feature explains why text was flagged, and it says it can detect AI-generated code. It offers a browser extension, a Google Docs add-on, learning-management-system integrations and an enterprise API.

Strengths: explanation of flagged text, code detection, broad integrations and published per-language accuracy figures, which range from 93.08 percent for Portuguese to 99.20 percent for English on AI text, according to the page.

Limitations and gaps: the figures are the vendor’s own. It claims a 0.03 percent false-positive rate and cites a 2023 study, so treat the number as a claim to verify on your data. Free scans cover up to 25,000 characters, but paid plan prices sit on a separate pricing page.

Fits: organizations that need multilingual coverage, code detection or integrations.

Originality.ai combines AI detection with a plagiarism checker and a fact and hallucination checker. It lists sentence-level highlights, a mixed AI and human category in its newer detection models, a Chrome extension with a writing replay feature and an AI detection API.

Strengths: several checks in one product, an API with documentation and a clear statement of limits. The page acknowledges false positives, says very short text under a 100-word minimum and AI rewriting tools can affect results, and advises against using the score alone.

Limitations and gaps: it is credit-based, free scans are capped at 100 credits per account and credits expire two years after purchase. Its accuracy claims cite third-party studies and internal benchmarks that you should review yourself.

Fits: publishers, agencies and SEO teams that want detection, plagiarism and fact checks in one workflow.

Turnitin is built for educators and institutions. Its AI writing detection estimates how much of a submission is human-written versus likely AI-generated, including likely AI-paraphrased content, and works inside learning-management systems alongside similarity checking.

Strengths: deep institutional integration and unusually explicit framing of results as probabilities. For documents above its 300-word minimum, the page reports false-positive rates of 0.014 for English language learners and 0.013 for native English writers and concludes there is no statistically significant bias. It also links guidance on handling suspected false positives.

Limitations and gaps: it is aimed at institutions rather than individual freelancers, the page does not give an overall false-positive figure, and it describes detection as just one piece of a broader challenge. Mention of language support is limited, with a linked post about Arabic.

Fits: schools and universities that already use Turnitin and want detection within the same workflow.

Sapling offers an AI content detector with a free check of the first 2,000 characters, and Pro and Enterprise accounts can check up to 100,000 characters. It provides a free API key and documentation, and it publishes unusually candid guidance on limits.

Strengths: transparent caveats and a developer-friendly API. The page says false positives and negatives may occur, that accuracy varies with dataset, text length and threshold, and advises measuring results on your own examples. It also warns that some tools claiming to be undetectable falsely say they passed its detector.

Limitations and gaps: accuracy improves after about 50 words, non-English text is scored by the English model for unsupported languages and is described as less reliable, and prices are not listed on the page. A reported 60 percent drop in false positives comes from internal evaluations that the page does not publish.

Fits: developers and teams that want to integrate detection and test it on their own data.

The table summarizes what each page states. It is not a benchmark, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

• False positives. Human writing can be flagged, especially when it is short, formulaic or highly predictable.

• Bias risk. A research paper titled GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers found that the detectors it tested consistently misclassified non-native English writing as AI-generated, and warned against using such detectors in educational settings. Turnitin’s page reports the opposite for its own tool, which is a reason to test on your population.

• Evasion. Paraphrasing or editing AI text can lower scores. The same research found that simple prompting strategies could both reduce bias and get text past detectors.

• Mixed authorship. A document that is partly AI-assisted can get a low overall score while individual sentences score high, as Sapling’s page points out.

• Moving targets. New models change the text distribution, so a tool trained on older models can lose accuracy.

• Shifting benchmarks. Vendors report different datasets and thresholds, so numbers are not comparable.

OpenAI’s own experience is a useful reminder. Its AI text classifier correctly flagged 26 percent of AI-written text on a challenge set while mislabeling 9 percent of human text, and the page states that the classifier was withdrawn on July 20, 2023 due to its low rate of accuracy. Detection has improved since, but the underlying difficulty has not gone away.

Most detectors are classifiers trained on large collections of human-written and machine-generated text. They look for statistical patterns, such as how predictable the word choices are or how uniform the sentence structure is, and output a probability. Some systems add features such as sentence-level scoring, writing-process data, or checks for hidden provenance signals.

• Statistical signals. Text that a language model finds highly predictable tends to look machine-like, which is why formulaic human writing can be misflagged.

• Trained classifiers. Detectors learn from labeled examples and update as new models appear.

• Writing-process evidence. Tools such as Writing Replay record how a document was typed or pasted, which is stronger evidence than a style score.

• Provenance. Standards such as C2PA Content Credentials aim to record the origin and edits of content when the creating tool supports them, which is different from guessing after the fact.

Because vendor figures are not comparable, the most reliable approach is to measure. Build a small labeled set that reflects your real content, including human writing from different groups of authors, and calculate false-positive and false-negative rates by group. The script below wraps any detector behind a single function. The stub is a placeholder, so replace it with a call to the tool you are evaluating and follow that vendor’s API documentation.

is_ai: bool        # ground truth you control

group: str = "all" # e.g. "native", "non-native", "technical"

def evaluate(detect, samples, threshold=0.5):

"""detect(text) -> probability the text is AI-generated (0..1).

Wrap any vendor API or tool export in this function."""

g = stats.setdefault(s.group, {"fp": 0, "human": 0, "fn": 0, "ai": 0})

g["fn"] += not flagged          # AI text that slipped through

g["fp"] += flagged              # human text wrongly flagged

fpr = g["fp"] / g["human"] if g["human"] else float("nan")

fnr = g["fn"] / g["ai"] if g["ai"] else float("nan")

print(f"{group:12} false positive rate {fpr:.1%}  false negative rate {fnr:.1%}")

return 0.9 if "delve" in text.lower() else 0.2

Sample("Let us delve into the topic.", True, "native"),

Sample("I wrote this note by hand.", False, "native"),

Sample("We delve into methods used here.", False, "non-native"),

Sample("The results were reviewed twice.", True, "non-native"),

With only a handful of samples the numbers mean little, so use a larger, representative set and report results per group, because an acceptable overall rate can hide a high rate for one group.

• Never treat a score as proof. Use it to start a conversation, not end one.

• Gather corroborating evidence. Drafts, version history, writing-process data and discussion with the author carry more weight than a percentage.

• Tell people how detection is used. Publish a policy so authors know what to expect and how to appeal.

• Check for bias. Test on writers like those you evaluate, including non-native speakers.

A tool that estimates how likely a piece of text is to have been generated by an AI model, usually as a percentage, often with sentence-level highlighting.

They can be useful, but accuracy depends on the text, length, language and threshold, and every vendor in this guide states that errors can occur. Test on your own samples.

Yes. False positives are acknowledged by vendors and documented in research, particularly for short or formulaic text and some non-native English writing.

Free tiers are fine for a quick check, but they have limits on length and features, and the result should not be the sole basis for a decision.

Sometimes. Paraphrasing and editing can lower scores, and partly AI-generated documents can produce mixed results.

A plagiarism checker looks for matches with existing sources. An AI detector estimates whether text resembles machine-generated writing, which is a different and less certain task.

AI detectors are useful screening tools, but none is a verdict. The six reviewed here differ in language coverage, limits, integrations, explainability and how candidly their pages describe error, and their accuracy figures come from different tests. Compare them on the factors that matter for your content, measure false positives on your own samples, and combine any score with other evidence before acting on it.

#10250. How Much Latency Does a Self-Hosted LLM Gateway Add? Langfuse vs LiteLLM vs AcruxCore

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A self-hosted LLM gateway sits between your app and the model provider, so every call pays for one extra hop. We measured that cost for three open-source gateways: the Langfuse AI Gateway, the LiteLLM proxy and AcruxCore. Each one ran on the same machine, in front of the same OpenAI model. LiteLLM added 61 to 67 ms to every non-streaming call. AcruxCore added 15 to 24 ms. Langfuse's number could not be told apart from zero.

The bigger lesson was about the measurement itself. Before we controlled for it, one OpenAI network address moved our results by more than any gateway did.

Each number is the median time a gateway added to a direct OpenAI call, with its 95% interval in brackets. A gateway can log each call, and logging takes time, so we ran the test three times with three logging levels.

The direct call took 781 to 831 ms at the median, so even LiteLLM's cost is under 9% of a short call. Read the tables this way:

The obvious test is to time 100 calls through the gateway, time 100 direct calls, and compare the two medians. That test gives the wrong answer, for two reasons.

The first reason is noise. OpenAI's own response time moved by hundreds of milliseconds between calls in our runs. The direct call's p95 was 1,047 to 1,233 ms against a median near 800 ms. A gateway that adds 20 ms is hidden inside that spread unless the test removes it.

The second reason is the network path to OpenAI. It does not stay the same between a direct client and a gateway, and that difference can be larger than the gateway itself.

api.openai.com resolves to more than one address. From our network, DNS returned two Cloudflare addresses, and one was much farther away than the other. We measured both with a script that pins one address at a time:

On a connection that is already open, both addresses answer in the same time. On a new connection, the far address adds about 250 ms, because the TCP and TLS handshakes take that much longer.

A gateway keeps its connection to OpenAI open between calls. It pays the setup once and then stays on whichever address it reached first. A client that opens a new connection for each call pays the setup again on every call. How much it pays depends on which address DNS returns that time.

Node's built-in fetch closes an idle connection after about 4 seconds. So a test client that calls OpenAI every few seconds reconnects on almost every call. In our first, uncontrolled run, the Langfuse gateway came out 43 ms faster than calling OpenAI directly. A gateway cannot be faster than the call it forwards. The direct client paid for new connections, and the gateway did not.

The fix has two parts. First, pin api.openai.com to one address on every path. In Docker, that is an extra_hosts entry on each gateway container:

Second, let the direct client keep its connection open, as a gateway does. With undici, the HTTP client behind Node's fetch, that is a custom Agent:

We then listed each container's open connections to confirm that every path used the same address. The edge-check script is in the repository linked at the end, and it takes about a minute to run from your own network.

This advice also applies outside benchmarks. If your app calls OpenAI directly from Node, keep the connection open between calls. Otherwise some of your calls pay the handshake, and on a far address that costs about 250 ms.

Each test sent 150 rounds after 5 warm-up rounds. One round calls OpenAI directly and through each gateway, once without streaming and once with streaming. The order rotates every round, so no path always goes first or last.

For each round, the script takes the gateway's time minus the direct call's time in that same round. Calls in one round are made within a few seconds of each other, so a slow moment at OpenAI hits all four paths together and cancels out of the difference. The script then reports the median of the 150 differences.

The interval comes from a bootstrap. The script draws 150 differences at random, with replacement, and takes their median. It repeats that 2,000 times, and the middle 95% of those medians is the interval. This is a shortened version of the script's function:

An interval that includes zero means the test could not separate the gateway's cost from zero. That is what the Langfuse rows show. It does not prove that the cost is zero.

Every call used OpenAI gpt-6-luna with reasoning_effort: "none", the same short prompt and a cap of 5 output tokens. A short answer keeps the model's own time small, so more of the measured time belongs to the path. Each streamed call measured the time to its first token. Each non-streamed call measured the time to the full response.

All three gateways did real work on every call, which made the comparison fair:

The three logging levels mapped to these settings:

The machine was an AMD Ryzen 9 5900X with 62 GB of RAM, running Fedora Linux and Docker 29.9. All three stacks ran on it at once, and the test was run on 10 November 2026.

LiteLLM added 61 to 67 ms to the full response, but only 9 to 43 ms to the first streamed token. The first token arrives as soon as the model starts to answer, so time spent before that point shows up in both numbers. The larger cost without streaming suggests that most of LiteLLM's extra time is spent after the model has answered. We did not profile LiteLLM to confirm this.

Logging level made no clear difference for any gateway. Adding LiteLLM's Langfuse callback did not raise its cost. AcruxCore's median rose from 15 ms with logging off to 24 ms with full logging, but its intervals overlap across all three runs. AcruxCore's median is 16 to 24 ms above Langfuse's, and those intervals overlap too, so this test does not rank the two of them.

If 60 ms per call matters to you, as in a chat app that makes several model calls per user message, LiteLLM's cost is real and repeatable. Langfuse and AcruxCore stayed near or within the noise. If your calls take several seconds, any of the three costs less than OpenAI's own variation from one call to the next.

Before you trust a gateway number, your own or anyone else's, check two things. Was each gateway compared with a direct call in the same round? And did the direct client keep its connection open on the same OpenAI address as the gateway? Without both, the result measures the network path and not the gateway.

The scripts, Compose files and raw results are on GitHub: scripts/comparison/langfuse-gateway-vs-litellm-vs-acruxcore.

Talha Anwar is a senior AI and full-stack engineer and writes about building and running AI systems.

#10245. CrowdStrike is buying Zscaler to create a cybersecurity giant built for the era of AI agents

Two cybersecurity companies are coming together in one of the industry’s biggest ever mergers.

On Monday, November 23, CrowdStrike announced that it will purchase Zscaler in an all-stock deal. The transaction values Zscaler at a whopping $43.9 billion, with the company’s shareholders getting 1.135 CrowdStrike common shares (Nasdaq: CRWD) for each Zscaler share (Nasdaq: ZS) they own.  

“Security used to be about keeping the adversary out. Today, safety is required to let AI in,” said George Kurtz, CEO and founder of CrowdStrike. “The network used to connect people to places. Now it connects agents to data.”

CrowdStrike stock falls, Zscaler rises

In response to the news, CrowdStrike’s shares fell more than 8% in premarket trading, while Zscaler shares rose over 17%. 

CrowdStrike expects the deal to expand its total addressable market by $185 billion, with the combined company bringing in over $10 billion in annual recurring revenue. 

Kurtz will stay on as CEO of the joint company, while Jay Chaudhry, founder and CEO of Zscaler, will lead Zscaler’s business and become a member of CrowdStrike’s board. 

The deal is expected to close in the second half of 2028, subject to regulatory approvals. It comes amid growing concerns over vulnerable tech infrastructure and a future of bot-fueled cyberattacks.

“With Zscaler, we’re building cybersecurity’s operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely,” Kurtz added. “We see a path to become the largest AI safety and security company the world has ever seen.”

Alongside the purchasing announcement, CrowdStrike and Zscaler both shared their quarterly earnings reports.

Kurtz called CrowdStrike’s most recent quarter the company’s best yet. CrowdStrike had record-high cash flow from operations with $665 million. Its revenue rose 28% year-over-year (YOY) to $1.58 billion. 

Similarly, Zscaler’s quarterly revenue rose 25% YOY to $898.2 million.

#10244. Samsung fans continue to hate on Galaxy S27 Ultra redesign

An alleged new video shows Galaxy S27 dummy units that look like the latest leaks, and Samsung fans aren’t having it.

At this point, it’s anyone’s best guess as to what the Galaxy S27 series looks like, but it’s seeming surer and surer that Samsung will be giving the series a big redesign this coming year. Chris Franklin, a writer at SammyGuru, posted an unboxing video of the Galaxy S27 on X, citing that there’s a possibility the unboxing is AI-created — there are some eyebrow-raising reflections here, but it’s hard to tell for certain. The design looks similar to the “confirmed” renders that leaked a few days ago, although there are some subtle differences.

I don't think much about the design of phones, they're essentially all the same, especially when considering you're looking at the front 90% of the time, but I've always found the Galaxy's vertical camera layout to be the least attractive of any of the major phones. I think this looks much better.

Unsurprisingly, another leak from earlier in the month has a similar look but, again, with subtle differences. So far, all the major leaks in the past few months are pointing to Samsung outfitting the Galaxy S27 series with a raised camera island that looks extremely similar to Apple’s design on the iPhone 17 Pro and 18 Pro series.

Samsung isn’t alone here. The Xiaomi 18 series and Honor Magic 9 Pro series both have eerily similar designs, and many other 2026 and 2027 phones have followed suit. The most obvious problem with Samsung’s potential design (and, by extension, Apple’s) is the raised camera lenses, which protrude above the raised camera island. Xiaomi’s island is flat, following Google’s idea that a camera bar should protect the lenses and also keep the phone from wobbling or feeling off-balance.

Drama has already taken off on X (formerly Twitter), where Noah Cat reposted the video, and it seems Samsung fans aren’t happy. Samsung has needed to change up the vertical camera bar for years, as it has regularly gotten in the way of Qi2 and MagSafe magnetic accessories. This new design might help that, but it seems fans wanted Samsung to return to the Galaxy S10 horizontal camera bar days, not this new iPhone-esque raised island.

#10243. Find Orphan Pages and Buried Content: Build an Internal Link Graph for Your Site

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The pages of a site form a graph. Think of it as many nodes connected to each other via edges. Each of the edges are the links between the pages, and the nodes themselves are the pages. Now if you start to visualize this as a graph, you will quickly see that there are multiple ways to traverse this graph and reach a particular endpoint.

A search crawler usually uses one of these pages as a starting point and crawls through all of the pages (especially when pages are not fully covered in a sitemap).

If a page lies very deep from the home page, it means that it's not an important page. It's an indication to the search engine that this is not something that you yourself consider important, and the search engine has a lesser incentive to rank this page over pages that are linked better within your site.

The key metric here is link depth. That is the number of clicks it takes to reach a particular page from your home page.

Another key metric is broken links. If you have too many broken links, it indicates to the search engine that your site is outdated and not well maintained, and the search engine will then not want to rank your site.

The way to identify both these problems is the same: to actually walk through your site, do a crawl of your site outside in, and try to figure out what the link depth is and if there are broken links on your website.

Seed the crawl with the home page and all URLs mentioned in the sitemap. Technically, the sitemap is not required if you're doing a crawl, but going from the sitemap will allow us to detect orphaned pages as well.

Fetch the pages and follow redirects as required. Record when you're following a redirect: we do not let fetch follow it silently, we record each hop and add its target to the crawl. Record HTTP errors as they occur.

Drop URL fragments and tracking parameters. Keep trailing slashes because sometimes there can be mismatches around expectation of trailing slashes in different URLs of a site.

In order to navigate from the home page, we can use BFS. So we know that the first time we reach a page, that is the page's shortest path.

We can cut off the depth over a certain threshold, say 5, to indicate that pages beyond that are too far or too deep to be reached.

Noindex pages will still be crawled. However, we need to make a record of them being not indexed, to reflect that they will not be present in the search engine.

The desired page depth is as close to the home page as possible. Important pages should be close to the home page. The deeper you go from the home page, it signals to the search engine that the page is less important.

A couple of examples of how a deep page is present:

The suggested fix for this is that we link the pages from as close to the home page as possible:

Wasted links are those internal links that do not do the job they're supposed to do. The different types of wasted links:

We have seen here how to look at our own website through the lens of a search engine. You can use some of the code over here to create your own crawler and identify internal linking issues; the full script is in this gist. Alternatively, we can use a free internal link visualizer to identify these issues and focus only on the fixes to improve our site's internal linking.

#10240. This is one of your kitchen’s hardest working tools. Here’s how to keep it food safe

The cutting board might be the hardest working tool in the kitchen yet one thought about least. It takes the raw chicken, then the onions, then sometimes the bread, and in between it typically gets a quick swipe with the nearest sponge.

If cutting boards are given a second thought, it’s usually in the debate over whether to use wood or plastic. But the more important issue is how to clean and care for the boards you already own.

“I think the real question is not which is safer, but are they both safe to use?” said Donald Schaffner, a professor of food science at Rutgers University who studies how bacteria move between surfaces.

Knife fight! Plastic vs. wood boards

For a long time, plastic was considered the safer choice, mostly because it seemed easier to clean. Then in the 1990s, Dean Cliver, a food safety researcher at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, put salmonella and E. coli on wood boards and found the bacteria were pulled down into the wood, where they didn’t multiply and eventually died off.

Plastic boards were easy to clean, but once they were all scratched up, bacteria-harboring residue like chicken fat settled into the knife grooves and was hard to scrub out by hand.

Schaffner said the research is “a bit muddied,” but Cliver’s work showed “wood was not as risky as we thought.” Wood also has natural antimicrobial compounds that seem to help, at least somewhat.

Nicole Papantoniou, senior director of the Kitchen & Cooking Lab at the Good Housekeeping Institute, doesn’t pick a side. She uses both.

Beyond wood and plastic cutting boards

Papantoniou is a fan of composite boards, made from wood or paper fibers bonded with resin. They’re light and they hold up.

One paper composite board made by Epicurean was a winner of Good Housekeeping’s 2027 Kitchen Awards. Epicurean CEO Dave Benson said knife cuts in composite stay open instead of closing back over bits of food the way they can on plastic, which makes the boards easier to clean.

Schaffner pointed out that there isn’t much independent research yet on how composite or bamboo boards stack up against wood and plastic.

Rubber boards, common in restaurant kitchens, are easy on knives but not many are made for home use, Papantoniou said.

Glass is nonporous, and she still wouldn’t recommend it: It slides, it can break and it dulls knives. And marble and slate look gorgeous under cheese and charcuterie, but don’t cut on them. “Your poor knife,” she said.

How to clean your cutting board

For everyday chopping, Papantoniou said washing with warm, soapy water and letting the board air dry is plenty.

But truly sanitizing takes an extra step. It should be done after a board has already been cleaned to kill bacteria the washing can leave behind.

Hot water from the tap isn’t going to get you there. “If the water were hot enough to actually kill bacteria, it would also burn our hands,” Schaffner said.

After raw meat or poultry, Schaffner sanitizes, either by carefully pouring boiling water over the clean board, running it through the dishwasher on the sanitize cycle or using bleach diluted according to the directions on the bottle. Vinegar and hydrogen peroxide “are not very effective, at least not nearly as effective as bleach,” he said.

Wood should be washed by hand, since the dishwasher or a long soak in the sink can warp or crack it. Plastic and composite boards can go in the dishwasher. It’s why Schaffner saves the plastic ones for raw meat and poultry.

Keeping separate boards for raw meat and produce is “a perfectly reasonable food safety precaution,” he said, but it’s not a must. Just remember that bacteria travel with water, so a wet chicken breast can spread them to the board, to your hands and to whatever you grab next (often the pepper grinder).

Extra care tips for wood boards

While they look great on a kitchen counter, wood does need more babying than plastic.

Papantoniou said wood boards should be oiled and kept conditioned. That’s less about food safety and more about keeping the board in good shape for years, and it’s a lot easier to keep up with if you start when it’s new. Wood boards should also dry standing on their edges so air can get to both sides.

John Boos & Co. has been making butcher block cutting boards in Effingham, Illinois, since 1887.

“Oil wood cutting boards once a month, and more often if you use them daily for meal prep,” said Lisa Bosio, vice president of group marketing at the company. When the wood looks lighter and a little dry, it’s due, she said. Boos recommends a food-safe mineral oil, applied in a light layer, left to soak in overnight and wiped off in the morning.

For stubborn stains, like those from tomatoes or beets, Noah Pinsonnault, home care and cleaning reviews analyst at the Good Housekeeping Institute, suggests 3% hydrogen peroxide left on for about five minutes and then rinsed off. Peroxide is a mild bleach and can lighten the wood, especially darker varieties like walnut, so try it on a small spot first.

If the board smells like last night’s garlic, scrub it with a paste of baking soda and water, rinse and let it dry completely, Pinsonnault said.

When to toss your cutting board

There’s no hard rule for when a board needs replacing. Schaffner gets rid of one when it becomes increasingly hard to get it visibly clean. Papantoniou tosses boards that warp, plastic boards with deep grooves or little curls that could end up in food, and wood boards that crack or develop dark spots that could be mold.

Katie Workman writes regularly about food for The Associated Press. She has written two cookbooks focused on family-friendly cooking, “Dinner Solved!” and “The Mom 100 Cookbook.” She blogs at https://themom100.com/. She can be reached at Katie@themom100.com.

—Katie Workman, Associated Press

#10239. Why Nvidia brought Jensen Huang back as CEO despite his scandals

It took just 11 days for Nvidia to reverse course on Jensen Huang, its totemic CEO, who is returning to his position as president and CEO, as well as a member of the board.

The decision also appears to have received the White House’s tacit approval, according to Nvidia’s surprise announcement of Huang’s return. That’s despite an ongoing independent investigation into whether Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence through a woman with whom he has acknowledged having an affair. And the controversy extends beyond that relationship: Huang has also faced allegations of at least one, and possibly two, other affairs with subordinates. During his brief absence from the company, he also faced criticism over his reportedly toxic management style.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said in a statement.

His return to power echoes Sam Altman’s brief sojourn outside OpenAI—an episode that marked its three-year anniversary last week—and highlights just how important individual leaders have become to the success of companies like Nvidia and OpenAI.

“It’s a stunning return,” says Kristy Loke, a research fellow at MATS studying China’s place in the broader AI world—and Nvidia’s role in the global geopolitics of AI. “It doesn’t necessarily mark the end of the chip debates in D.C., but it speaks to the centrality of Jensen as the chief strategist for Nvidia and as the force that’s holding the many pieces of the AI ecosystem together.”

That centrality was evident in the groundswell of support for Huang’s reinstatement across Silicon Valley over the past week. A veritable who’s who of tech executives spoke up for him. Elon Musk was among those calling for Huang’s return on November 14, warning that many of Nvidia’s most important supply-chain deals rested on personal relationships with Huang rather than written contracts. Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick also backed him, arguing that his mistakes did not warrant removing him from the company he built. By November 16, a petition calling for Huang’s reinstatement had attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including those of Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, and more than 8,800 people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees.

Nvidia’s board appears to have reached a similar conclusion about Huang’s integral role in running the company, owing in large part to his hands-on management style. “This is a board that reversed itself because the alternative, a founder-less Nvidia at the start of the Rubin cycle with a CEO search running into next year, was the bigger risk to shareholders,” writes Dan Ives, principal analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co.

Nvidia is partway through launching its Rubin chip platform, with updates due later this year—a process Huang will likely want to oversee closely, given that the platform has already generated $20 billion in its first quarter of production. “It chose to pair the reversal with the governance architecture investors will want to see around him,” Ives adds.

Ives has attempted to put a price on Huang’s importance. In his estimation, Nvidia is worth $300 a share with Huang back in charge and its governance troubles resolved, versus $225 without him—a difference of a third. Even so, he has maintained his formal price target of $225 while the investigation continues.

Investors also appear confident in Huang’s return, with Nvidia shares surging nearly 30% in the first few minutes of trading following the announcement.

Huang’s 11 days in the wilderness were more than twice as long as Altman’s absence from OpenAI, but his grip on Nvidia appears no less significant. As Fast Company previously reported, the skills and responsibilities any permanent replacement would need to master make for a daunting list. They include balancing the competing interests of the White House and Beijing while managing a complex web of informal relationships with Taiwanese suppliers—relationships that have helped cement Nvidia’s seemingly unassailable lead in the AI chip race.

It’s Huang’s relationship with Washington that may have proved most important, reckons MATS’ Loke. “Trump’s presidency in his second term is very much an AI presidency,” she explains. “The same goes for the American stock market. Huang is the key node, through circular financing, support for the open model ecosystem, and also being a key supplier of AI hardware.”

“He is, it seems in hindsight to some,” Loke adds, “in fact irreplaceable.”

#10236. A 1992 Batmobile is going to auction, but don’t expect to see it out on the road

It was hijacked by the Penguin, careened through Gotham’s streets and lived beneath Wayne Manor. Now it can be yours — if you have a Bruce Wayne-sized bank account.

The Batmobile — one of three custom-made versions used in Tim Burton’s 1992 blockbuster “Batman Returns” — will hit the auction block Monday in Gardena, near Los Angeles, as the centerpiece of a Julien’s Auctions sale that features dozens of pieces of Batman and other superhero memorabilia.

With a preauction estimate of $5 million to $7 million, the vehicle could break the Batmobile auction record set in 2013, when the car driven by Adam West in the 1960s TV series sold for $4.6 million including fees.

Known as the “Number One Hero car” and measuring just under 20 feet (about 6 meters) long with two sweeping tail fins, the glossy black vehicle appeared in the majority of the film’s driving sequences, Julien’s said in auction notes on its website.

Since then it has spent years on display at the Marconi Automotive Museum in Tustin, California. It still has its original paint, Chevrolet V-8 engine and radio-controlled flaming exhaust system that Michael Keaton’s Batman used to torch one of the Penguin’s circus goons.

Citing the influence of Burton’s “darker aesthetic” on modern superhero movies, Julien’s called the car “one of the most recognized and important cinematic vehicles in Hollywood history.”

No matter who buys this Batmobile, don’t expect to see it on the road: Julien’s noted that the vehicle is “not street legal” and the engine and transmission have been tested a “limited number of times” since filming concluded.

The buyer must also adhere to various restrictions, according to an agreement with Warner Bros. Consumer Products Inc., which handles DC Comics’ intellectual property rights.

For example the buyer must secure approval before exhibiting it at special events, and the vehicle “must remain stationary when exhibited to the public,” the auction house said.

—R.J. Rico, Associated Press

#10234. Young Americans can’t afford to move out. These cities are seeing the biggest increases

A near-record share of young adults won’t be traveling home to visit family for the holidays—they’re already living there.

One in three U.S. adults between age 18 and 34 live with their parents, according to a new report from Realtor.com. That’s 25.2 million or 33% of young adults living at home in 2025, only a sliver less than the 33.6% during the pandemic-era peak in 2020. 

Living at home is one way that Americans who can’t afford to buy or rent on their own wrestle with the high cost of housing and other expenses. While the cost of housing is a nationwide problem, the share of adults living with their parents offers an interesting glimpse into regional affordability patterns around the country.

“The pattern of young adults at home has spread beyond the most expensive markets, with the share rising most in parts of the South and West, including some that have traditionally supported an earlier launch,” Realtor.com’s chief economist, Danielle Hale, wrote in the report. “As young people adapt to high housing costs, they are delaying homeownership and the wealth creation that comes with it.”

Two stories with the same ending

Predictably, at least one of the country’s priciest cities is among those with the largest share of adults living with their parents—but the full story is more complicated. New York leads the list, with 41.3% of adults between the ages of 18 and 24 staying in the nest. In Philadelphia, Miami, Baltimore, and Houston, more than 38% of adults in that age range lived with their parents. Across Los Angeles, Atlanta, and Chicago, the share of adults living at home was over 35%. 

Houston, Atlanta, and Baltimore aren’t known for their high cost of living, unlike costly urban hubs like New York and Los Angeles, but home prices have soared in recent years in those markets. That rapid change to local affordability is freezing many young adults out of a housing market they might have been able to afford during a previous era.

The share of adults living at home has grown the quickest in Las Vegas, San Francisco, and San Jose, but those metros tell different stories. In San Francisco and San Jose, two expensive cities close to the AI boom, housing prices have always been high, even as they grow higher still. In Las Vegas, once known as a relatively affordable market in the West, home prices have skyrocketed by more than 60% since 2019.

“Las Vegas and the Bay Area show two different paths to the same challenge,” wrote Hannah Jones, senior economist at Realtor.com. “In Las Vegas, the sharp rise in home prices has made it harder for young adults to buy. In San Francisco and San Jose, already-high housing costs and limited inventory leave many young adults facing steep barriers to living on their own.”

Living at home on the rise

Regionally, the Northeast still dominates with 36.9% of young adults living at home in 2025, though that number is trending down. The West is next with a 32.4% “co-residence” rate, followed by 32.3% in the South and 31.7% in the Midwest. 

That share is rising everywhere except the Northeast, demonstrating that the housing affordability crisis may look distinct in different corners of the country, but it’s something that a surprising share of Americans everywhere are struggling with.

“For young adults who hope to live independently or buy a home, elevated costs and limited entry-level supply can delay household formation and, for would-be buyers, the opportunity to build home equity,” Jones said. “Until affordability improves and entry-level supply expands, the report finds that pent-up demand is likely to continue accumulating.”

#10233. Microsoft is shutting down the ‘To Do’ app that replaced Wunderlist, with no real replacement

Microsoft announced this week that its To Do app is shutting down soon, taking the legacy of Wunderlist with it.

Microsoft is shutting down its To Do app at the end of June 2027, with focus moving to the newer Planner app. The company explains:

As we bring personal task management into Planner, we will phase out To Do. The To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027. Connections that other apps use to access To Do tasks will continue beyond that date, and we’ll provide separate notice before those connections are retired. We’re also updating existing task integrations across Microsoft 365 to connect with Planner, so you’ll be able to create or manage tasks in the Microsoft experiences you already use. Although To Do tasks are already visible in Planner, they will not be migrated to the new private plan. Customers using personal Microsoft accounts will need to choose another app. Our To Do transition guidance  will help you understand what’s changing and plan your next steps.

To Do was built on the foundation of Wunderlist, a wildly popular to do list app that Microsoft purchased in 2015. Wunderlist later shut down in 2020.

Microsoft’s shuffle, notably, leaves general consumers without a replacement app. To Do was available to anyone with a Microsoft account, where Planner is available only to enterprise/business users. So, for long-time Wunderlist users who followed Microsoft migration, this is the end of the road and it’s officially time to move to another app.

#10230. After Anthropic’s record-breaking debut on Wall Street, nonprofits prepare for a wave of AI philanthropy

It was philanthropy, the story goes, that first bonded two of the founders behind artificial intelligence giant Anthropic.

Jared Kaplan, the San Francisco company’s chief science officer, and CEO Dario Amodei were doctoral students carpooling to an event organized by an academic fellowship. As Kaplan recalls, he and Amodei spent the ride discussing “this idea of thoroughly investigating what kinds of charitable causes could do the most good.”

“We had so much largesse to, sort of, disperse,” Kaplan joked at a Hertz Foundation discussion in April 2025.

Those once-hypothetical philanthropic ambitions gained new steam as Anthropic debuted on the stock market to a record $1.5 trillion valuation. The Claude AI tool maker already plans to dedicate 5% of its shares for a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund. Its seven co-founders say they’ll give away 80% of their equity — a $112 billion commitment based on its IPO price.

Now suddenly affluent employees, many of whom will become millionaires as they sell their vested stock, may wield enough capital to make transformative donations themselves — riches that are commanding the attention of nonprofits looking to direct some sliver toward causes from global health to animal welfare.

Silicon Valley has great expectations. The napkin math suggests leading U.S. AI firms’ valuations could add at least $37 billion annually in intended philanthropy, according to a widely circulated May blog post by Nan Ransohoff, head of public goods at the payments company Stripe.

“This is a once-in-a-lifetime kind of opportunity for people to really make an impact on extreme poverty,” said Peter Singer, the moral philosopher whose writings influence many tech donors.

Nonprofits aren’t counting on an immediate charitable windfall, though. Many Anthropic employees cannot sell or gift the bulk of their shares until next spring. Questions persist about the charitable priorities of these potential philanthropists whose worldviews have been shaped by the increasingly powerful AI models advancing at breakneck speed. The sector’s volatility — between high borrowing costs, recent turmoil at the chipmaker Nvidia and warnings about risks to humanity — leaves skeptics doubtful about the amounts actually available to redistribute.

“The challenge is that deploying philanthropic capital is hard,” said Renaissance Philanthropy president Kumar Garg, whose nonprofit matches funders with scientific initiatives. “That’s not an automatic step.”

AI philanthropists are expected to make large donations quickly

Will the artificial intelligence wave of wealth creation differ from previous ones that created new philanthropy?

There’s reason to believe so, according to Benjamin Soskis, a historian of philanthropy and senior research associate at the Urban Institute’s Center on Nonprofits and Philanthropy, even if he finds the number of tech executives who have “actually managed to empty the safe” is low.

The modern philanthropic foundation stemmed from the post-Civil War wave of industrial capitalism. Titans such as oil magnate John D. Rockefeller Sr. and steel tycoon Andrew Carnegie established bureaucratic institutions intended to address the root causes of social problems. Those were followed by the turn-of-the-century technology wealth that brought a more data-centric, risk-taking approach. The Gates Foundation launched to address pressing crises in global health and poverty.

AI wealth, according to Soskis, carries a sense of “extreme peril” and “really transformative promise” that should spur even more urgent action from this emerging class of donors.

At least one of Anthropic’s co-founders will donate in the coming weeks to the Trump Accounts children’s savings program, according to comments made Friday by U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on CNBC.

Anthropic’s explosive growth is also fueling some anticipation that its 5,300 employees will want to rapidly scale their charitable impact, too. A generous internal giving program adds another incentive. Employee equity gifts are matched by the company with shares of Class N common stock. Anthropic also partners with donor-advised fund vendors such as Daffy, which offer a tax-efficient tool for grantmaking without the hassle of a more sophisticated charitable foundation.

Daffy CEO Adam Nash expects this younger generation to give more quickly.

“The people working in AI see the impact AI is having already,” Nash said. “And they are giving now, right?”

Tech-adjacent nonprofits prepare for influx

One organization in particular appears poised to move those rising donation volumes.

Coefficient Giving was formed by San Francisco-based billionaire Cari Tuna and her husband, Dustin Moskovitz, a Facebook co-founder and early Anthropic investor. A spokesperson told The New York Times the couple transferred their Anthropic stake into an undisclosed nonprofit last year to avoid personally profiting.

The philanthropic funder — which has directed more than $8 billion since 2014 in support of global health, animal rights, AI safety and the effective altruism community — has been scaling its pledges. In July, Coefficient Giving increased its commitment to the grantmaker GiveWell to $1 billion.

The move reflected expectations of “considerably more future funding for this kind of work,” according to the announcement.

“We might grow a lot, in part because we want to spend faster in response to these trends,” Coefficient Giving CEO Alexander Berger said during a late July public discussion. “But there is a great deal of room for other organizations and approaches, and I do not expect us to play an overwhelmingly dominant role.”

GiveDirectly has spent months identifying the biggest barriers to rapidly growing its antipoverty work, according to Nick Allardice, its president and CEO. The tech-focused nonprofit sends cash straight to poor households with no strings attached.

Recipients must have mobile phones to receive the digital transfers. GiveDirectly offers phones for about $15, usually subtracted from recipients’ first payment. So the nonprofit secured investments this year to build out a supply chain to support many more mobile phones going forward.

The group is betting that its preparations for a charitable boom will be worthwhile.

“I have this level of cautious optimism,” Allardice said. “But I can’t foresee the future, and I don’t know exactly what’s going to happen.”

Wild Animal Initiative executive director Cameron Meyer Shorb shares those tempered expectations.

His nonprofit funds wild animal welfare research. It’s the sort of work some observers predict will see the biggest upswings in support: nonprofits connected to effective altruism, a data-driven movement that prioritizes donations to causes with the greatest impact on the most living beings.

The movement’s reputation took a hit when Sam Bankman-Fried, one of its leading proponents and financial backers, got a 25-year prison sentence for cryptocurrency fraud. But the ideas are rebounding in the same tech circles that could see big payouts as more AI companies go public.

Effective altruists have learned not to rely too heavily on any one funder, according to Shorb. He expects “quite a bit” of fresh support for animal advocacy and sees an outsize role for midsize donors.

He said he has connected with a couple of Anthropic employees. Perhaps more important, he said, are relationships with the philanthropic advisers who help plan donors’ giving.

“As you can imagine, it’s a pretty tricky place for a soon-to-be billionaire to be to have all this potential power coming soon,” Shorb said. “As soon as anyone finds out about that, anyone who can possibly get their email or phone number will just be knocking down their door. So we’ve tried to be gentle and slow and respectful in our approach.”

—James Pollard, Associated Press

#10229. Running an AI Agent on a Local LLM: What I Measured on One GPU

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Running an AI agent on your own GPU sounds simple: point it at Ollama and stop paying per token. I set up OpenClaw, an open-source AI assistant, with a 9B model in Ollama on one RTX 3090 and connected it to Discord. Then I read the Ollama log for every request.

The agent worked. The numbers were not what I expected, though. A one-line question turned into a prompt of more than 18,000 tokens, the first reply took over a minute, and the small model sometimes guessed instead of using its tools.

This article covers what I measured and what each number means if you plan to run an agent on local hardware.

OpenClaw ran in Docker and reached Ollama on the host at http://host.docker.internal:11434. Discord was the chat interface, and OpenClaw's web panel showed the sessions and context use.

This article is about the results, not the installation. The full step-by-step setup is in a separate guide to running OpenClaw in Docker with Ollama and Discord. That guide covers the Compose file, the Discord bot and how to keep the ports off your network.

All timings below come from the Ollama log on the test machine. Ollama loaded the model with a 32,768-token context.

My first message in Discord was short: "Which model are you running on, and what is 17 * 23?" The bot answered correctly: it ran on ollama/qwen3.5:9b, and 17 × 23 is 391.

The Ollama log showed what that question cost. The model processed 18,415 prompt tokens and generated 33 tokens.

The extra tokens come from the agent itself. With every request, OpenClaw sends:

On the RTX 3090, reading that prompt took 10 seconds at 1,838 tokens per second. A slower GPU, or a CPU, needs much longer to read the same prompt.

Prompt tokens per model call, from the Ollama log. Only the first message had to process the whole prompt.

OpenClaw counts tokens with its own estimate, which was higher than the Ollama count. The gateway log estimated the prompt at 24,608 tokens, against a prompt budget of 24,576 tokens for this model. By OpenClaw's own count, the base prompt alone used up the budget before any conversation history.

The web panel showed a similar figure: 68 to 69 percent of the context window was in use for the Discord sessions after only a few messages.

The first message arrived while the model was not loaded in GPU memory. That reply took 1 min 10 s:

Reply times on the test machine. Loading the model took most of the first reply.

The speed-up comes from prompt caching. The system prompt, tool definitions and workspace files at the start of the prompt stay the same between requests. Ollama kept that part cached and processed only the new tokens. The model wrote at 91 to 96 tokens per second in every test.

Ollama's documentation says models stay in memory for 5 minutes by default before they are unloaded. After that, the next message pays the load time again. You can change this with the OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE environment variable on the Ollama server, or with the keep_alive parameter per request. A negative value, such as -1, keeps the model loaded. I did not change this setting in the test.

If you run Ollama in Docker, pass the variable with -e OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=-1 or in the environment: section of your Compose file.

Two things used the GPU besides my chat messages.

A heartbeat. OpenClaw's web panel listed one scheduled automation, heartbeat-main, which runs every 30 minutes. The agent wakes on that schedule, so the model gets called even when nobody chats. With Ollama's 5-minute default, the model is unloaded between heartbeats unless someone chatted recently, so a heartbeat most likely starts with a model load. I did not measure this.

An embedding model. During the first message, OpenClaw also called Ollama's /api/embed endpoint twice to index its memory. It used qwen3-embedding:4b, which was already installed on the Ollama server. I did not set OpenClaw to use that model; it picked it on its own.

The two models took this much GPU memory:

That is 11.4 GB for the models alone, almost half of the RTX 3090's 24 GB.

What this means for you: plan GPU memory for the chat model, the embedding model and the context, not the chat model alone. If the GPU also runs other models, the heartbeat can compete with them.

The first two tests in Discord: a question, then a file written with a tool. The user name is blurred.

The mistakes showed up when the model had to check something:

After the restart, the bot claimed it had lost the earlier session. When asked to use its read tool, it read the file correctly.

The fix for the first problem was simple. When I wrote "use your read tool to open homelab-test.md", the model opened the file and listed all three points correctly. Naming the tool made it check instead of guess.

The model listed four files and missed the test file and a folder, because it answered from its prompt.

Based on this test, a local 9B model on one consumer GPU works for:

If you need better answers, OpenClaw also works with hosted models, but then your prompts leave your machine.

In this test, qwen3.5:9b used 6.3 GB and the qwen3-embedding:4b memory model used 5.1 GB. Together the two models needed 11.4 GB.

The model had to load into GPU memory first, which took 59 seconds of the 70-second reply. Ollama keeps a model loaded for 5 minutes by default, and the OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE setting changes that.

Every request includes OpenClaw's system prompt, its tool definitions and its workspace files. A one-line question became an 18,415-token prompt in this test.

Yes. A heartbeat automation runs every 30 minutes and calls the model even when nobody sends a message.

It handled questions, arithmetic and file creation correctly in this test. It sometimes answered from its prompt instead of using its tools. When it wrongly said its memory was lost, asking it to use its read tool made it check the file and answer correctly.

#10228. The free market isn’t so free. Just look at Jensen Huang

There’s plenty to scratch your head about in the speedy and surprising return of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO, just 11 days after he resigned following revelations of an affair with a woman who may have helped make him a target of Chinese intelligence. Never mind the fact that two other allegations of improper relationships with Nvidia employees have emerged, alongside a slew of claims about his reportedly toxic management style. Or that he’s still, technically, under investigation, according to Nvidia’s statement announcing his return. Or that six days earlier, the board told investors it “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”

Perhaps most head-scratching of all is the White House’s claim to reporters that “President Trump was totally involved” in Huang’s return to the company, and reports that he dialed into a board meeting to argue for the return of the executive whose resignation the board had accepted less than two weeks earlier. Trump has since claimed in a call to CNBC following the announcement that Huang was “exonerated”—before adding, almost incongruously, that “he’s in the business of selling chips.” (That leap between one thought—the basis for which remains unclear, given the unfinished independent investigation—and another tells its own story.)

Senator Elizabeth Warren has called the decision “reckless.” There’s another word for it that might come to mind. But the most diplomatic way to say it is that it’s the end of a free market in the United States.

Leaders of countries can have their own opinions about who should run a major company operating in their country. But they shouldn’t be influencing boardroom discussions about the running of that company. Nvidia’s own announcement acknowledges that directors received “input from senior levels” of the U.S. government before concluding that Huang’s reinstatement posed no national security risk.

The massive losses in the stock market, with Nvidia a lynchpin of the AI boom, won’t have gone unnoticed at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue. And for a man who professes to be the master of “the art of the deal,” a deal that boosted Nvidia’s market value by roughly $1 trillion in a matter of hours sounds like a pretty sweet deal.

But rising share prices don’t answer questions about Huang’s conduct, or his paramour’s potential ties to Chinese intelligence. Nor do they explain why a supposedly independent board tasked with holding executives accountable appears to have allowed a world leader to influence its deliberations and ultimately sway its decision. Trump, after all, explicitly said he “convinced them” to reinstate Huang.

And what about the Nvidia employees on the receiving end of Huang’s reported tirades? According to The New York Times, he has threatened to rip off employees’ arms and beat them to death with them, tear the tops of their heads off and “pee on your brain,” and told one employee that his mother should have aborted him. To be sure, many Nvidia employees have expressed support for Huang. But at least when Sam Altman was deposed as CEO by his board at OpenAI nearly three years ago to the day, the groundswell of opinion in favor of reinstating him represented a near-unanimous employee revolt.

The truth is that Jensen Huang may ultimately be cleared of the most serious allegations being made against him—that’s literally what investigations are for. But the independent investigation hasn’t concluded. And some of the most powerful people in America seem to have arrived at the verdict first, and decided the process can catch up later. That’s not a free market. But it is a big, beautiful trade.
